note: Records are bullet lists from sections Executive principles, 1.3 and 2.3; id prefix shows the origin.

records.text: Specificity: train the quality the user wants to improve. Strength, hypertrophy, endurance, power and sport performance overlap but are not interchangeable.
Progressive, repeatable training beats novelty. Choose a plan the user can execute consistently and recover from.
Individualise dose. There is no single universally optimal split, set count, rep range, weekly frequency or cardio zone for every user.
Use the minimum useful complexity. Beginners usually need simple movements, manageable volume and repeatable progression; advanced users may need more precise loading and fatigue control.
Safety first. Screen for red flags and relevant health constraints; do not diagnose or prescribe rehabilitation.
Separate factual retrieval from personality. Humour may change the delivery, never the scientific answer or safety response.
External torque changes across an exercise's range; a machine, cable, free weight and band can load a muscle differently even when the named movement looks similar.
Stable exercises often make it easier to direct effort toward a target muscle; free-weight and complex movements can add coordination and skill demands.
Concentric actions shorten the muscle under load; eccentric actions lengthen it under load; isometric actions produce force without visible joint movement. All can contribute to training adaptations.
Neuromuscular adaptation, skill learning, muscle size, connective-tissue adaptation and cardiovascular change occur on different timelines.

ATP-PCr supports brief high-power efforts; glycolytic metabolism contributes to hard efforts lasting longer; oxidative metabolism supports sustained work and recovery. Energy systems overlap rather than switching on one at a time.
Double progression: keep a rep range; when all work sets reach the top of the range with target RIR and good technique, increase load modestly and rebuild reps.
Add sets only when progress stalls and the user is recovering well; first check adherence, technique, sleep, exercise setup and whether the current stimulus is already sufficient.
Progress one or a small number of variables at a time: load, reps, sets, range of motion, density or exercise difficulty.
Record load, reps, sets, RIR/RPE, pain flags and session completion. A plan generator needs longitudinal data to adapt responsibly.
Do not force weekly load increases. Maintain or reduce load when technique, readiness or recovery suggests it.
